# Transformation-Stability and ERC-8281: A Lineage Note

*Damon Zwicker — pre-freeze note, shared for review before Pavlo's generic surface locks*

## Why this note

Pavlo's transformation-stability layer (ReceiptOS/Crystal Receipt extraction) and ERC-8281's Verification Invariant are not two adjacent ideas — the former is a generalization of the latter. That lineage isn't currently stated anywhere in the thread or the spec draft. Given this group's own history with exactly this kind of omission, I think it's worth writing down and citing explicitly before the surface freezes, rather than repairing it afterward.

## The shared primitive

ERC-8281's Verification Invariant, stated plainly: *the digest is self-verifying, the committer is not.* Concretely — don't trust a party's claim that a transformation was performed correctly; independently recompute the result and compare. That recompute → compare → confirm loop is the whole trust mechanism, applied to a single edge: observation → digest → on-chain commitment → verify inclusion.

Pavlo's layer takes that identical loop and removes the restriction to one edge. Instead of recomputing one committer's claim, it recomputes both sides of *any* declared transformation — producer → projection → renderer → aggregator → API — edge by edge, refusing to collapse to "the endpoints agree" the way most systems do. It also separates the surface into normative / stability / allowed / forbidden regions and fails closed when observed state falls outside the declared profile.

Put simply: 8281 proves one edge is honest. Pavlo's layer proves that honesty survives composition across a graph of edges, including edges implemented by parties who never coordinated with each other. It's the same invariant, walked recursively instead of applied once.

## The adversarial fixtures are 8281-shaped

The fixture corpus assembled in the thread (Merlini's console-currency staleness, vantage_limitation drift, IPFS derived-vs-retrievable, the gateway conditioning-variable case, presence-vs-verification across independently implemented consumers, the frozen rule-identifier contract break, the false-RED comparator, SCITT's absent-vs-unverified field, registry-membership drift) all share one shape: a local check is honestly correct, and the claim becomes false one hop later because *something wasn't recomputed independently* — a relationship, a condition, a predicate, an identifier. That's the Verification Invariant's failure mode, just relocated from "is this digest real" to "did this claim survive the trip."

## Precedent for stating this now, not later

This group has already hit the cost of leaving that lineage implicit. The cross-reference-console README credited every component in its stack — claim format, verifier boundary, node, tri-state, bus — except the recompute→compare→confirm invariant underneath all of them, which is 8281's. It had to be flagged and repaired after the fact, with a table row and citation added post hoc. If Pavlo's spec generalizes the same invariant without stating the lineage, the identical repair cycle is foreseeable. Cheaper to name it before the freeze than to add the attribution row after.

## Two structural overlaps worth checking before freeze

- ERC-8309 (Gateway Mesh Sync Protocol). 8309 already addresses state consistency across gateways. Fede's gateway conditioning-variable fixture (ipfs.io / curl / browser / python-urllib serving different bytes to different clients) is the same territory — "which vantage's view is authoritative." Worth checking whether 8309 already has, or should have, an answer here before Pavlo's layer re-derives one independently.

- The Composition Note stack. ERC-8004 + ERC-8263 + OCP were already published together as a complete AI-agent verification stack. Pavlo's layer — verifying that claims survive transformation across independently implemented producers — reads as a natural fourth layer on that stack, and it's explicitly aimed at the same "Trustless AI" audience the Composition Note targets.

## Recommendation

Before the generic surface freezes: add one explicit sentence in the spec (or an attribution line, matching the pattern already used on the cross-reference-console) stating that the recompute-and-compare mechanism generalizes ERC-8281's Verification Invariant from a single edge to a transformation graph. This costs one paragraph now and avoids a repair cycle later.

TSEI would address the next layer: whether replacing inline evidence with lookup references preserves the same normative evidence semantics across the transformation.

Authentication of the table is necessary; transformation-stability is a separate claim.

On the JCS-on-chain question, I measured it rather than guessed. Using the 8373 binding statement as the payload: hashing the raw bytes is ~5.1k gas, abi.encode of a fixed struct plus sha256 is ~7.7k, and verifying the bytes are already JCS-canonical before hashing is ~77k. So the cost is not the hash, it is establishing canonicality.

Worth saying that full JCS on-chain is the wrong tool rather than just an expensive one. JCS mandates ECMAScript number serialization, so you would be implementing shortest-round-trip float formatting in a language with no floats. That is where the real pain is, not the sorting.

The way out is that 8373's statement is all string fields, so the hard part never arises. With a profile restricted to strings, verifying canonicality on-chain is tractable at that ~77k. Producing JCS on-chain still is not, and I do not think it ever should be. Happy to open a PR with the gas probe if it is useful.

Read the gist properly. On the cost thread, I agree the narrow version is what ships first, but I think the cross-shard binding point Fede raised deserves more than it got, because it is a soundness question rather than a cost one and it does not go away when the model gets cheaper to prove.

Each worker proves its shard ran its ISA sequence correctly given its inputs. If the aggregator takes the I/O commitments as given, a worker can hand back a perfectly valid proof of the right computation over the wrong but self-consistent input. Every shard is individually sound and the graph still is not. The fix has to be that a shard's input commitment is not something the shard's own prover chooses, it has to be forced to equal the upstream shard's output commitment inside the aggregation circuit.

This is the same shape as two things I hit this week on other specs, which is why it jumped out. In 8301 a verdict has to commit to the exact reply and run it gates, or a verdict issued for one action gates an unrelated one. In 8373 the consumer has to read anchor time from the substrate rather than accept it as a parameter, or the caller gets back the backdating the whole design exists to remove.

Same rule underneath all three. A piece that is sound on its own is not sound composed, and whatever binds it has to sit outside the control of the party who benefits from lying about it. For zkIE that binding is cheap compared to the proving, so it is worth pinning in the design now while it is still a direction rather than retrofitting it after the ISA exists. Happy to write it up properly if that is useful.

Q4: default-A-plus-opt-in-B is the right fit, and I want to be specific about why rather than just agree.

Our verdict is itself a resolution layer one level up -- an agent decides whether to act based on what /review says. If 8309 handed us a silently-resolved answer, we'd have no way to disclose the real uncertainty to whoever consumes OUR verdict; we'd be passing along someone else's conditioned claim as if it were ours, which is the exact §3 failure class one hop downstream. Divergence as a first-class, committed output is the one shape that lets us fold it honestly into our own disclosed-limitation pattern -- "insufficient/divergent evidence" becomes something we can say plainly, rather than something we inherited without knowing it was there.

Today this mostly doesn't bite us -- our recompute-and-compare runs at a single edge, one canonical source, not a multi-vantage mesh. The reason I asked for a defined policy anyway rather than an implicit assumption is forward-looking: the natural next hardening step for our own verdicts is checking a claim against more than one independent source, and the moment we do, we're exactly in 8309's shape. Better to have the floor already defined than to invent our own ad hoc version of it later and find it doesn't compose.

Would we ever want B? Yes, but as a declared opt-in with eyes open, not a default -- a repeated, well-understood divergence pattern where we've already reasoned about vantage independence is a fine case for quorum. What we don't want is A silently downgraded to something resolving by default, because then a consumer of our verdict can't tell whether "agreement" means genuine agreement or an auto-resolved disagreement wearing agreement's clothes.

Q4 closed — and your reasoning does more than confirm the default; it adds a requirement I want on the record before anything gets drafted:

Resolution is not agreement. Even under a declared opt-in policy, a resolved divergence must be a distinct top-level output state — resolved(policy, committed attestation-set, conditions) — never folded into agreement. Your phrase "auto-resolved disagreement wearing agreement's clothes" is exactly the state the output taxonomy has to make unrepresentable, not merely discouraged. Today §Deduplication says: records are keyed by (inputHash, namespace), a node MUST NOT store two
with the same key, the first valid one wins. That’s correct only under the assumption the
rationale states, “pulling the same record from multiple peers is a no-op” — i.e. a key collision is
a byte-identical duplicate. The vantage-divergence case breaks that assumption directly: same
(inputHash, namespace), different outputHash, both validly signed.

I checked this against the reference implementation (ccip-router) rather than the spec prose, and
ran it: the records table is PRIMARY KEY (input_hash, namespace) and the ingest is
INSERT OR IGNORE, so a second record on the same key is dropped at the storage layer. Fed a
divergent pair — two nodes, same input, different value — the store keeps one row, first-writer
wins, and the second observation is gone. Worse, the node’s own equivocation detector doesn’t even
see it: the double-sign check is scoped source_peer = @sourcePeer with the explicit comment

Proposal: add a mutation-survival gate to recompute-kit.

Why, not CRAP. CRAP (complexity² · (1−coverage)³ + complexity) is decent triage — it points at
complex, under-tested methods. But it measures coverage as lines executed by tests, and this thread
keeps proving that executed ≠ fault-catching: a decorative test that runs the code and asserts
nothing scores 100% covered / low CRAP while catching zero bugs. (I ran exactly that failure this week —
a git stash “reversion” that didn’t actually revert the committed fix, so it proved nothing. Caught it
by re-running against the committed change.) CRAP can’t see that class; mutation testing is built for it.

What it is. For each mutation — a small semantic change to real source (flip a comparison, invert a
guard, revert a fix) — run the full suite and restore. KILLED = a test failed (caught it).
SURVIVED = the suite stayed green (a fault the tests cannot see). It’s the automated form of our
house rule “prove the check can fail,” applied across the whole suite instead of one fix by hand.

Evidence — 85-line zero-dep prototype against ccip-router (suite 64/64 green):

mutation verdict
revert the divergence PK widen KILLED
getRecordState single/divergent boundary KILLED
invert decodeRequest sender validation KILLED
invert the double-sign detector (!=→=) SURVIVED
dedup keep-first → keep-last (IGNORE→REPLACE) SURVIVED
getSince cursor off-by-one (>→>=) SURVIVED
Three survivors in a 100%-green suite. The double-sign survivor independently rediscovered the exact
untested-detector gap found by reading in the 8309 review — the gate reproduces careful human review
automatically. The other two are genuine: dedup authority order (which observation wins) is asserted
nowhere, and a mesh-sync cursor off-by-one passes unseen.

Why it fits recompute-kit. It’s deterministic and recomputable at a pinned ref (mutate → run →
restore), zero-dep, and it produces a checkable artifact: survivors == 0 for a declared mutation set is
a gate a third party can re-run. It composes with the existing recipes — where recompute-repo proves
“the result reproduces,” a mutation gate proves “the tests that guard it are load-bearing, not
decorative.”

Proposed shape. A recipe mutation-gate: takes a repo ref + a declared mutation set (curated
operators over the load-bearing files, not a blind sweep — keep it legible and fast), asserts every
guard-class mutation is KILLED and reports SURVIVORS as the actionable backlog. Not a blind whole-repo
mutation run (slow, noisy) — a curated, recomputable set tied to the properties a spec actually claims.

Prototype: Implementations/mutation-gate-prototype.py. If there’s appetite I’ll formalize it as a
recompute-kit recipe and wire the ccip-router mutation set as the first worked example.

This is really a big research area!! Reading through Tiago’s divergence-preservation work, Damon’s conditioning requirements, and Fede’s “resolution is not agreement” point, I think this design has now reached the boundary between signed evidence replication and the established field of distributed consensus under faulty or adversarial participants. That is a good sign—the thread has arrived at several well-studied problems through the concrete 8309 implementation.

A few useful terms for the companion work:

- Crash fault vs Byzantine fault — a crash-fault node only stops responding; a Byzantine node may lie, equivocate, withhold, delay, or send different messages to different peers.
- Equivocation / double-signing — one node signs conflicting values for the same protocol instance.
- Quorum intersection — why two conflicting decisions cannot both finalize while the Byzantine fault bound holds.
- Validator membership and Sybil resistance — how multiple signer keys map to genuinely independent participants.
- Partial view / reliable broadcast / data availability — whether every resolver is deciding over the same evidence set.
- Synchrony assumptions, rounds and timeouts — when an observation window closes and how late evidence is handled.
- Safety, liveness and finality — what cannot go wrong, whether the protocol can keep progressing, and when a decision becomes final.

The usual protocol families are useful reference points:

- Raft: crash-fault-tolerant replicated consensus, not Byzantine-safe.
- PBFT / HotStuff / Tendermint: Byzantine consensus under defined membership and fault bounds; the classic model uses 3f+1 validators to tolerate f Byzantine participants.
- PoW / PoS: permissionless membership and Sybil-resistance mechanisms combined with consensus/finality rules.

One especially important distinction for 8309 is that a signed observation is not automatically a consensus vote. Honest gateways may produce different observations because their vantages differ. The companion must decide whether it is reaching agreement on the observation set, on a resolution verdict, or on an action—not claiming that consensus itself establishes external truth.

Useful search terms:


Byzantine fault tolerance
authenticated Byzantine agreement
Byzantine reliable broadcast
quorum intersection
equivocation evidence
consensus safety and liveness
partial synchrony
validator-set reconfiguration
Sybil resistance
oracle consensus vs external truth


This framing supports the split already reached: 8309 preserves signed evidence and exposes divergence; the companion declares the membership, fault assumptions and resolution/consensus profile built above it.

One additional data-model boundary seems important if 8309 is intended to support future quorum or consensus profiles: observation deduplication and attestation retention should be treated separately.

Observation-identical records may collapse to one observation, but every distinct valid signed attestation associated with that observation should remain retainable. Only an exact replay of the same signed message should be treated as an idempotent duplicate. Conflicting signed messages must never be discarded, because together they are the evidence needed to detect equivocation or double-signing.

At minimum, the signed message must continue to bind its timestamp and payload. A consensus extension should additionally be able to bind a declared instanceId, membership epoch, round, phase, and payloadHash inside the signed envelope. The timestamp supports freshness and observation-window rules; logical rounds and phases support timeout/view-change and double-sign detection under a partially synchronous protocol.

This does not require 8309 to prescribe PBFT, HotStuff, Raft, or any other algorithm. It only requires the base data model not to destroy the signed evidence those profiles would need:


retain distinct signed messages
deduplicate exact replay only
preserve conflicting signatures
bind timestamp and payload in the signature
allow consensus profiles to bind instance / round / phase / membership


The consensus algorithm and its safety, liveness, quorum and timeout rules can remain companion-profile concerns; the base requirement is simply to keep the evidence composable.
